models_evaluated: hypothetical AI-enabled smartwatch/smartphone app for atrial fibrillation detection (simulated labels)

links.outcome: Effect of AI label information elements on patient trust and acceptance
links.effect: Regulatory approval, high performance, HCP oversight, and added value raised trust by 14.1%-19.3% and acceptance by 13.3%-17.9% (AME); safety management info not significant.
links.quote: The discrete choice experiment showed that information about regulatory approval, high device performance, provider oversight, and AI's value added to usual care significantly increased the likelihood of patient trust by 14.1%-19.3% and acceptance by 13.3%-17.9%.

links.outcome: Patient comprehension of AI label prototypes and information elements' effect on understanding
links.effect: 86.7% found labels easy to read, 84.2% easy to understand; information elements had no significant effect on legibility, comprehensibility, or overload.
links.quote: Most participants reported that the AI labels were easy to read (perceived legibility; 86.7%) and understand (comprehensibility; 84.2%).

links.outcome: User reactions (credibility, effectiveness, trust, intention to use) to AI disclosure label content
links.effect: Provider oversight, regulatory approval, performance, added value improved credibility/effectiveness (OR 1.35-2.05), reduced doubts (OR 0.61-0.77), increased trust/intention to use (OR 1.47-1.73).
links.quote: The single profile factorial experiment showed that patients reported good label comprehension, and that information about provider oversight, regulatory approval, device performance, and AI's added value improved perceived credibility and effectiveness of the AI label (odds ratio [OR] range: 1.35-2.05), reduced doubts in the AI device (OR range: 0.61-0.77), and increased trust and intention to use the AI device (OR range: 1.47-1.73).
